content: Lesson 17 gave the imperfect: an action
under way in the past. The PERFECT names
the other kind — one act, done and shut.
Six endings hang on a stem of the verb's
own, and they belong to no other tense:
cōnsīderāvī       = I considered
cōnsīderāvistī    = you considered
cōnsīderāvit      = he considered
cōnsīderāvimus    = we considered
cōnsīderāvistis   = you all considered
cōnsīderāvērunt   = they considered
Lēgātus perīcula diū cōnsīderāvit.
= The legate considered the dangers
for a long time.
-vit against -bat: did it, against was
doing it.
The perfect runs on a stem of its own,
not on the present one. Many are plain:
-āre   cōnsīderāvit   considered
-ēre   habuit         had
-ere   dīxit          said
-īre   audīvit        heard
Others rebuild the word altogether.
Lesson 23 takes those up.
sum runs on fu-: fuī, fuit, fuērunt.
Watch the third person plural. -ērunt is
perfect; the bare -unt of dūcunt is
present. One letter parts the two.
English hides this tense under two forms:
'they took' and 'they have taken' are
both cēpērunt.
The perfect stem does not stop at one
tense. Two more are built on it, and
neither asks for a new stem.
The PLUPERFECT sets a past before a past.
Perfect stem, then the endings of eram:
dēcesseram     = I had withdrawn
dēcesserās     = you had withdrawn
dēcesserat     = he had withdrawn
dēcesserāmus   = we had withdrawn
dēcesserātis   = you all had withdrawn
dēcesserant    = they had withdrawn
Dēcesserat et possessiōnem trādiderat.
= He had withdrawn and had handed the
holding over.
Both acts closed before the story's own
past began. -era- is the mark to catch.
The FUTURE PERFECT sets one future act
before another. The same stem again, now
with the endings of erō:
dēcesserō       = I shall have withdrawn
dēcesseris      = you will have withdrawn
dēcesserit      = he will have withdrawn
dēcesserimus    = we shall have withdrawn
dēcesseritis    = you all will have withdrawn
dēcesserint     = they will have withdrawn
Sī dēcesserit, oppidum capiēmus.
= If he withdraws, we shall take the
town.
Latin marks the earlier of two futures
where English lets a present stand.
One stem, three tenses: -ī for the
perfect, -era- and -eri- for these two.
A Latin verb is quoted with four parts.
The third is the one this tier turns on:
ferō, ferre, tulī, lātum
videō, vidēre, vīdī, vīsum
capiō, capere, cēpī, captum
1 I do it       2 to do it
3 I did it      4 done
The third part holds the perfect stem.
Cut its -ī and every perfect, pluperfect
and future perfect follows: tul-, vīd-,
cēp-.
Ager magnōs frūctūs tulit.
= The field bore great crops.
tulit is ferō. Nothing in the sentence
says so; the third part is where it is.
Perfect stems are made a few ways, and
the shapes are worth knowing on sight:
-vī, -uī     cōnsīderāvī, habuī
long vowel   videō → vīdī, legō → lēgī
an -s-       dēcēdō → dēcessī
doubling     fallō → fefellī
a new word   ferō → tulī, sum → fuī
The last row is the one that stings.
tulī shares nothing with ferō, and fuī
nothing with sum. They are learned as
they stand.
Recognition only: meeting an unfamiliar
shape and asking which known verb owns
it. A card's Notes name the third part
whenever the answer is not on the page.
quī, quae, quod opens a clause that
describes the noun just before it: 'the
envoy WHO came', 'the war WHICH they
waged'.
Two rules pull in different directions.
Gender and number come from the noun
outside, the one being described.
Case comes from the job the word does
inside its own clause.
Lēgātus quī vēnit...
= The envoy who came...
Lēgātus quem vīdimus...
= The envoy whom we saw...
One envoy, two cases: quī is the subject
of vēnit, quem the object of vīdimus.
m.      f.      n.
subject      quī     quae    quod
object       quem    quam    quod
of           cuius   cuius   cuius
to or for    cui     cui     cui
by or with   quō     quā     quō
plural       quī     quae    quae
object pl.   quōs    quās    quae
Argūmenta quae dīxit vēra erant.
= The proofs which he gave were true.
argūmenta is neuter plural, so quae is
neuter plural too. Inside its clause it
is the object of dīxit — and for neuters
the object matches the subject.
A relative seldom shares its noun's case.
Core closes where it opened, with the
small words. Lessons 7 and 8 named them
when a sentence ran four words long.
et, -que, atque    and
sed, nōn           but, not
cum, ut, sī, quod  when, so that, if,
because
enim, nam, igitur  for, for, therefore
iam, tum, nunc     already, then, now
Nothing new is added here. What has
changed is the traffic around them: a
relative clause, a perfect or a
pluperfect, a preposition governing its
case, all inside one sentence.
The connective is the first thing to
read, not the last. It says what the
clause on its way is for.
Haec eadem ratiō est in summā tōtīus
Galliae.
= The same principle holds for Gaul
as a whole.
Now the same joints at full length:
Lēgātus dēcesserat; tum cīvitās quae
fīnitima erat arma cēpit, nam pācem
iam nōn spērābat.
= The envoy had withdrawn; then the
neighboring state took up arms,
for it no longer hoped for peace.
Read it by its signposts. tum sets the
order; quae hangs a description on
cīvitās; nam brings the reason.
Five roles, four conjugations, the
perfect family, the relative clause.
